transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Lee: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're gonna do a deep dive on quantization tradeoffs, runtime impacts, and deployment implications - mostly focused on the 7B/13B line for Halcyon's chat stack. Maya and Connor from our SE team are here.
[00:12] Dr. Anika Rao: Great, thanks. High level: latency SLO is 200ms p50, cost target is to cut token cost by ~40% without dropping NLG quality more than 3-4% on our classification/eval set.
[00:25] Maya Patel: Cool, that's helpful. Quick qual question - are you currently running FP16 on GPU or mixed CPU/GPU?
[00:33] Luis Mendes: FP16 on A100s in prod, but we're exploring lighter racks for inference - that's why quantization. We also have a private VPC, so on-premish eventually.
[00:43] Jordan Lee: Perfect. We'll walk through INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ tradeoffs and then hit runtime behaviors - KV cache, batching, and kernel selection can change observed latency a lot.
[00:58] Tom Bianchi: One quick ask - we need to know KMS/HSM implications for private deploys.
[01:05] Connor Wu: We'll include that in the security package, but short answer: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations, HSM in most on-prem footprints, and audit logs for key operations. We'll share details after this call.
[01:17] Maya Patel: Ok, starting with accuracy - INT8 quantization (naive per-tensor) tends to have larger regressions on generative tasks. GPTQ/GPT-Q (some people call it GPT-Q) and AWQ approaches that do per-channel/per-layer quantization and calibration tend to preserve quality much better.
[01:33] Dr. Anika Rao: We've run a few open-source GPTQ tools and saw ~6-10% drop on our contrived summarization eval on 13B - that's too high.
[01:42] Maya Patel: Right, that matches what we've seen. AWQ and later GPTQ variants can often get to within 1-3% for many tasks, but it depends on prompt distribution and outlier layers. Also FP8 (bfloat-ish FP8 or FP8 formats) can sometimes give a middle ground - better accuracy than INT8 and much smaller memory than FP16, but library/kernel support is newer.
[02:03] Luis Mendes: So FP8 will require specific kernel support on the runtime side - is Redwood's runtime supporting FP8 kernels now?
[02:11] Connor Wu: We have experimental FP8 paths on our dedicated runtime for certain backends and model types - it's not universally enabled. For production we typically recommend GPTQ/AWQ 4-bit or 8-bit flows unless you need exact FP8 behavior for research.
[02:25] Jordan Lee: Important note: the runtime will pick kernels based on sequence length distribution and hardware. If you use FP8, we may see different perf characteristics - e.g., reduced memory swaps but slightly different compute throughput.
[02:40] Maya Patel: On the accuracy side, our recommended checklist: 1) baseline FP16 eval on your representative prompts (you have that), 2) try GPTQ/AWQ with per-layer calibration and compute perplexity + downstream metrics, 3) inspect top-n token differences on failure cases, 4) optionally try mixed strategy (first N layers int8 awq, last layers fp16) - hybrid usually helps.
[03:05] Dr. Anika Rao: That hybrid idea sounds promising. Does Redwood support mixed precision within a single model runtime?
[03:12] Connor Wu: Yes, the serving runtime can use mixed kernels per layer; we expose quantization profile configs for that. It's an advanced config but we can precompute a recommended profile based on your evals.
[03:23] Luis Mendes: Performance question: with smaller quantized models, what's the expected throughput increase and latency change if we keep batch size 1? Our p50 requirement is strict.
[03:33] Maya Patel: If you keep batch size 1, quantization mostly helps memory and can reduce kernel execution slightly. Throughput increases more with batch sizes >1 because compute becomes more efficient. However latency p50 at batch 1 can improve modestly (5-20%) depending on KV cache behavior.
[03:49] Jordan Lee: KV cache is a big one - with client-side caching or prefix caching at the runtime layer, subsequent tokens can be much faster once KV is warmed. But quantization of KV tensors matters - some quantization strategies store KV in reduced precision which speeds memory bandwidth but can affect retrieval fidelity for long context.
[04:07] Dr. Anika Rao: We've seen hallucination increase on longer chats after quantization; could that be KV degradation?
[04:13] Maya Patel: Yes, possible. If KV quantization introduces noise in attention keys/values, the model may attend incorrectly and produce more hallucinations or degrade coherence. That's why we recommend measuring long-context tasks separately and possibly keeping KV in higher precision (e.g., fp16) while quantizing weights.
[04:31] Tom Bianchi: Is there a storage/IO impact for prefix caching if KV stays fp16?
[04:36] Connor Wu: Yes, keeping KV in fp16 increases memory footprint for cache; we recommend hybrid - keep KV fp16 for long context flows, quantize weights and activations for token generation compute. This is supported in the runtime via separate buffer policies.
[04:50] Luis Mendes: Okay. About batching strategies - static batching vs dynamic batching? We need low tail latency but also want cost efficiency.
[04:58] Maya Patel: Dynamic batching is good for throughput and cost but increases tail latency unpredictably. We recommend a two-tier policy: synchronous fast-path for low-latency calls (batch size 1, hot path) and async batching pool for background/cheap calls. Redwood Dedicated can allocate a small pool for hot-path to guarantee latencies.
[05:18] Jordan Lee: Also kernel selection matters - some kernels are optimized for long seqs or for specific batch sizes. Our runtime auto-selects kernels based on observed traffic but you can pin a policy if you want deterministic behavior.
[05:31] Dr. Anika Rao: Auditing/compliance - if we do private deployment, are we able to run quantization tooling on-prem and keep artifacts off-cloud?
[05:39] Connor Wu: Yes, Redwood Private supports running the full quantization pipeline in your VPC/on-prem. We can give you a package that runs GPTQ/AWQ locally and uploads results to your S3 (or on-prem object store). Key materials (weights, calibration) can be kept inside your environment.
[05:55] Tom Bianchi: Any caveats on GPUs - do we need specific CUDA versions for AWQ?
[05:59] Maya Patel: Some AWQ kernels rely on newer CUDA and cuBLAS versions; we provide a compatibility matrix. We'll include it in the follow-up. For example, certain 4-bit tensor cores require CUDA 12+ on Ampere/ADArch or else fallback slower kernels.
[06:15] Luis Mendes: Does Redwood do regression monitoring post-quant? E.g., automatic evals that trigger rollback if quality drops?
[06:21] Jordan Lee: Yes, Redwood Optimize includes quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets. For Dedicated/Private you can integrate your eval set and we can trigger canary rollouts and automatic fallback to FP16 model if regressions exceed thresholds.
[06:35] Dr. Anika Rao: About GPTQ vs AWQ naming confusion - our internal engs tried GPT-Q toolchain and AWQ seemed better on some metrics. Any rule of thumb?
[06:44] Maya Patel: GPTQ (original) is good but some forks and AWQ innovations improve calibration and per-channel scaling. In practice, AWQ often gives better downstream metrics on chatty generation tasks, but it's data dependent. We recommend running both on your sample set; that's why we'll run Maya's calibration job and compare.
[07:02] Sophie Carter: For our PM: when we say "within 3%", is that measured on perplexity or downstream metric like exact match or F1?
[07:09] Maya Patel: Downstream metrics are better - perplexity doesn't always correlate with task-specific quality. We'll measure both but prioritize your user-facing metrics.
[07:19] Jordan Lee: Practical next step: Halcyon provides a 500-prompt eval + baseline FP16 outputs. Maya will run AWQ/GPTQ on the 13B model and return a spreadsheet comparing top-n differences, perplexity, F1, latency, and token cost. We'll also include a suggested hybrid profile.
[07:36] Dr. Anika Rao: Sounds good. Also please include notes on KV-caching policy and recommendations for keeping KV fp16 for our long context sessions.
[07:44] Connor Wu: We'll annotate the spreadsheet with KV recommendations and expected memory/IO tradeoffs.
[07:49] Tom Bianchi: Final: VPC on-prem networking - we'll need a short checklist for firewall rules, peering, and SAML/SSO setup for Redwood Console.
[07:58] Jordan Lee: We'll include that in the security package.
[08:02] Dr. Anika Rao: Ok thanks, that'll help us decide whether to go AWQ or FP8 for our pilot.
[08:08] Jordan Lee: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the security package, benchmark spreadsheet, and schedule the on-prem pilot.
[08:12] --- End of meeting transcript (auto-generated). Notes: transcription contains occasional mis-attributions and minor typos as typical of automated transcripts.
